DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
STATE PANEL
On April 16, 2025, Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) Joseph Moy issued a
Recommended Decision and Order (“RDO”) finding Respondent Chief Judge of the Circuit Court
of Cook County (“Employer”) in default and concluding that Respondent violated Sections
10(a)(1) and 10(a)(2) and, derivatively, 10(a)(1) of the Illinois Public Labor Relations Act, (“Act),
5 ILCS 315/1 et seq. The Employer timely filed exceptions to the ALJ’s recommendations
contained in the RDO. Charging Party did not file a response to the appeal.1 After reviewing the
RDO, the record, and the Employer’s exceptions, we accept the ALJ’s recommendations contained
in the RDO but modify the remedy, as discussed below.
Charging Party Dorothy Ward filed the underlying unfair labor practice charge on
November 27, 2024, alleging that the Employer’s actions violated Section 10(a) of the Act when
it interfered with the exercise of Charging Party’s Weingarten rights and then retaliated against
1 Charging Party submitted an email to the Board’s General Counsel asking about the next steps in the proceedings.
Although she included assertions regarding union representation at meetings and retaliation for participating in
protected activity, she did not specifically respond to the Employer’s exceptions.
1

her for asserting those rights. The charge was investigated, and a Complaint for Hearing
(“Complaint”) issued pursuant to Section 1220.40 of the Board’s Rules and Regulations
(“Rules”). According to the Complaint, Charging Party is employed by Respondent in the title
of Mediator or “Conciliator Counselor” and is a member of the bargaining unit represented by
the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees, Council 31 (“Union”).
During the relevant time period, Charging Party served as a steward for the Union.
The Complaint details communications and actions occurring during the period October
8, 2024 through November 14, 2024. It alleges that the Employer denied Charging Party’s request
for a Union representative during an October 18, 2024 investigatory meeting and issued her a
verbal reprimand for insubordination related to that meeting in violation of Section 10(a)(1) of
the Act. The Complaint further alleges that the Employer retaliated against Charging Party in
violation of Section 10(a)(2) and (1) of the Act.
The ALJ’s conclusion that the Employer violated the Act was based on finding it in
default for its failure to answer the Complaint within the 15-day timeframe set forth in Section
1220.40(b) of the Rules. The ALJ observed that the Complaint was served on the Employer on
February 14, 2025, by electronic mail to its counsel, Vincent Waller, and contained the following
statement:
RESPONDENT IS HEREBY NOTIFIED that within 15 days after
service of the complaint upon it, pursuant to Section 1220.40(b) of the Board’s
Rules and Regulations, 80 Ill. Admin. Code §§1200-1300, it must file an answer
to this complaint with Joseph Moy, at the Illinois Labor Relations Board, 160
North LaSalle Street, Suite S-400, Chicago, Illinois 60601, or electronically at
ILRB.Filing@Illinois.gov in accordance with Section 1200.5 of the Board’s
Rules and Regulations. Respondent must serve a copy of the answer upon
Charging Party. Please note that the Board’s Rules and Regulations do not allow
electronic service of the Answer upon Charging Party. Said answer shall
include an express admission, denial, or explanation of each and every
2

allegation of this complaint. Failure to specifically respond to an allegation shall
be deemed an affirmative admission of the facts or conclusions alleged in the
allegation. Failure to timely file an answer shall be deemed to be an admission
of all material facts or legal conclusions alleged and a waiver of hearing. The
filing of any motion or other pleading will not stay the time for filing an answer.
He observed that under Section 1220.40(b) of the Rules, the Employer was required to
file an answer to the Complaint, no later than March 3, 2025, but failed to do so by that date.
Consequently, on March 14, 2025, the ALJ issued an Order to Show Cause (“Order”) to the
Employer as to why it should not be held in default for failing to answer the complaint within the
15-day timeframe. In response to the Order, the Employer’s counsel attached a “Response to
Charging Party’s Complaint” that he claims was timely filed when it was submitted to the Board
agent investigating the charge (“Investigator”) on December 2024, but did not also submit it to
ILRB.Filing@Illinois.gov.
Construing the Employer’s response to the Order as a request for leave to file a late answer
to the Complaint, the ALJ denied the request. Citing Board and court precedent, the ALJ observed
that that the Employer’s stated reasons for failing to answer the Complaint amounted to attorney
inattention or negligence and did not constitute the “extraordinary circumstances” needed to allow
a late filing under Section 1220.40(b)(4) of the Board’s Rules. Furthermore, although the
Employer did not request a variance from the Rules, the ALJ determined that the criteria for
granting a variance could not be satisfied under these circumstances.
As a result, the ALJ found that the Employer defaulted and waived its right to a hearing
by failing to answer the Complaint within the prescribed 15-day period set forth in Section
1220.40(b) of the Board’s Rules. And because the Employer failed to answer the Complaint
within the allotted time, the ALJ found that pursuant to Section 1220.40(b)(3) of the Rules, the
Employer admitted all material facts and legal conclusions alleged in the Complaint and
3

determined that the Employer committed the unfair labor practices as alleged. The ALJ then
concluded that the Employer violated Section 10(a)(1) and 10(a)(2) and, derivatively, 10(a)(1)
of the Act and recommended that the Employer be ordered to cease and desist engaging in unfair
labor practices, post notice of the violation, and notify the Board of the steps it has taken to
comply with the order. We note, however, that the ALJ inadvertently omitted rescission and
removal of the verbal reprimand given to Charging Party for insubordination as a remedy.
Because the Employer failed to answer the Complaint, it has admitted the conclusion that it
retaliated against Charging Party by issuing a verbal reprimand to her, forming the basis for the
Section 10(a)(2) violation. As such, to make the Charging Party whole, we modify the remedy
to include the rescission of the verbal reprimand and its removal from Charging Party’s record.
The Employer filed four exceptions and a supporting brief and contends that:
1. The material facts alleged in the complaint and deemed admit-
ted do not support, and in fact, contradict the conclusions of law
in Section IV of the RDO[;]
2. The RDO errs in disregarding “other grounds traditionally re-
lied upon for equitable relief from judgments[”;]
3. The RDO errs in construing Section 1200.160 as the exclusive
mechanism for exercising discretion[; and]
4. Deeming the material facts and conclusions of law alleged in
the complaint admitted is an abuse of discretion.
The Employer contends that the ALJ erred by failing to exercise discretion and excuse
the failure to answer the Complaint as required by the Rules. Section 1200.160 of the Rules
allows the Board to grant a variance from the Rules so long as certain criteria are met:
a) the provision from which the variance is granted is not
statutorily mandated;
b) no party will be injured by the granting of the variance; and
c) the rule from which the variance is granted would, in the
particular case, be unreasonable or unnecessarily burdensome.
80 Ill. Adm. Code §1200.160. The Employer, however, has not satisfied the third criterion.
4

In seeking relief from application of the Rules in the answering of complaints, the
Employer mainly relies on the Illinois Appellate Court’s decision in Cook Cnty State’s Attorney
v. Ill. State Labor Relations Bd., et al., 292 Ill. App. 3d 1 (1st Dist. 1997) to support its
contentions. The Employer contends that, as in Cook Cnty State’s Attorney, its response to the
underlying unfair labor practice charge submitted to the Investigator demonstrates that the
Employer has a meritorious defense and that there are mitigating circumstances sufficient to
excuse its failure to answer the Complaint within the 15-day timeframe. The Employer also
questions whether the Board has considered its response submitted to the Investigator and seeks
variance from the Rules to allow additional time to “file a response to the complaint and/or [an]
opportunity for a hearing in this matter. The Employer also points to Section 1220.40(b)(4),
asserting that there are extraordinary circumstances sufficient to excuse its counsel’s neglect.
The Employer’s contentions are unavailing. The Employer’s reliance on Cook Cnty.
State’s Attorney in seeking to excuse its failure to answer the Complaint is unpersuasive because
that case is readily distinguishable. In Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney, the court found that the
Board abused its discretion by failing to grant a variance and accept the State’s Attorney answer
which the court found was filed only three hours late and would have been timely filed had the
State’s attorney mailed its answer. Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney, 292 Ill. App. 3d at 13 (finding
that “[i]n this case, the answer was filed approximately 3 hours late. Had the State’s Attorney
mailed its answer on December 12, 1995, [the fifteenth day], it would have been deemed
timely.”).
Here, the Employer did not, and still has not, filed an answer to the Complaint, much less
filed one within the brief time period at issue in Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney. Instead, applicable
here is the court’s decision in Wood Dale Fire Protection Dist. v. Ill. Labor Relations Bd., et al.,
5

395 Ill. App. 3d 523 (2nd Dist. 2009), which involves facts more closely resembling the facts in
this case. In Wood Dale Fire Protection Dist., the court upheld the Board’s denial of a variance
where the respondent “waited 28 days after the deadline to file an answer, and, even then, after
it had been alerted to its mistake, did not request a variance for another 24 days.” Wood Dale
Fire Protection Dist., 395 Ill. App. 3d at 532. The court also observed that the respondent only
cited its attorney’s mistake for the delay and offer no explanation for the additional delay in
requesting a variance. Id. The court found that such mitigating circumstances were “far less
compelling than those presented in Cook County State’s Attorney and the delay was far more
than the three hours presented in filed Cook County State’s Attorney.” Id. at 533. Notably, the
respondent in Wood Dale Fire Protection Dist., eventually filed an answer.
But that is not the case here. In response to the ALJ’s Order, the Employer asserted that
its counsel timely filed a “Response to the Charging Party’s Complaint” in December of 2024
but neglected to copy ILRB.Filing@Illinois.gov. The Employer also attached the “Response to
the Charging Party’s Complaint” to its response to the Order. The Response to the Charging
Party’s Complaint, however, is clearly not an answer to the Complaint. The Employer admittedly
submitted a position statement to the Investigator in December 2024, over two months before the
Complaint issued in February 2025. The Board, through its agents, the Investigator and
Executive Director, considered the Employer’s response to the charge submitted in December
when investigating the charge and issuing the Complaint pursuant to Section 1220.40(a) of the
Rules. 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1220.40(a). The submission of the position statement in response to
the Order, however, does not transform the position statement into an answer to the Complaint.
Section 1220.40(b) requires a respondent to admit, deny, or explain each allegation or issue of
the complaint and to serve a copy of its answer on the Charging Party. The document that the
6

Employer submitted in response to the ALJ’s Order does not comport with the requirements of
Section 1220.40(b) of the Board’s Rules. It does not answer every allegation of the Complaint
nor is there any evidence or contention that the Employer served this document on the Charging
Party. Thus, the document the Employer filed in response to the Order cannot be deemed an
answer to the Complaint.
On exceptions, the Employer attributes its failure to file an answer to its counsel’s
negligence, asserting that mitigating circumstances exist to justify a variance. The Employer’s
counsel asserts that he missed the email attaching the Complaint “due to a deluge of forwarded
emails coming from the Director level employee’s email account” and was out of the office when
he received the ALJ’s Order which he “mistakenly believed” was prompted by his failure to send
its position statement to the Board’s electronic filing address in addition to the Investigator.
Although the ALJ construed its response to the Order as requesting leave to file a late answer,
the Employer did not seek leave to file an answer until now. Notably, the Employer does not
seek leave to file an answer to the Complaint instanter. Rather, the Employer merely seeks a
variance from the Rules for an unquantified amount of time to file an answer, without explanation
for the further delay.
Moreover, the Employer contends that we should grant a variance based on the existence
of similar mitigating circumstances—burden on the taxpayer and conflict with the efficient
operations of the Office of the Chief Judge—that the court in Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney found
noteworthy. In reversing the Board’s refusal to accept a late answer or a variance, the court in
Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney took note of the State’s Attorney’s reasons for discharging the
employee and found the reinstatement of an employee who was fired for neglecting her duties as
a victim specialist, to be a burden on the taxpayer and at odds with the State’s Attorney’s mission
7

in excusing the three-hour delay in the filing of the answer. Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney 292 Ill.
App. 3d at 12.
Here, the Employer does not explain how the ALJ’s recommended remedy, a notice
posting, presents a burden to taxpayers or interferes with the Employer’s mission. Moreover,
even though we have modified the recommended remedy to include the rescission and removal
of the verbal reprimand for failing to attend a meeting, it is difficult to see how requiring the
Employer to do so would present a burden to the taxpayers or conflict with the Employer’s
mission.
Finally, the Employer’s primary contention that the Complaint fails to state a claim is
meritless. The Employer has not answered each and every allegation and issue stated in the
Complaint and as a result, all of the Complaint’s factual allegations and legal conclusions are
deemed admitted. 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1220.40(b)(3). Moreover, the Employer does not seek a
variance from that section, and we decline to do so on our own motion.
For the above reasons, we accept the ALJ’s recommendations contained in the RDO,
subject to the modification to the remedy as described above.
IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that the Employer, its officers and agents, shall:
1) Cease and desist from:
a. Interfering with, restraining, or coercing the Charging Party in the exercise of her
rights by the Act when the Charging Party requests for a Union representative
during investigatory meetings.
b. Retaliating against the Charging Party for protected concerted activity of
requesting a Union representative attend the meeting with her and her supervisors.
c. Retaliating against the Charging Party to discourage membership in or support for
the Union.
d. In any like or related manner, interfering with, restraining or coercing its employees
in the exercise of the rights guaranteed them in the Act.
8

2) Take the following affirmative action necessary to effectuate the policies of the Act.
a. Make Charging Party whole by rescinding the verbal reprimand issued on
November 14, 2024, to Charging Party for insubordination and removing the same
from Charging Party’s employment records.
b. Post, at all places where notices to employees are normally posted, copies of the
Notice attached to this document. Copies of this Notice shall be posted, after being
duly signed, in conspicuous places, and be maintained for a period of 60
consecutive days. The Respondent will take reasonable efforts to ensure that the
notices are not altered, defaced or covered by any other material.
c. Notify the Board in writing, within 20 days from the date of this Decision, of the
steps the Respondent has taken to comply with this order.
BY THE STATE PANEL OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD

NOTICE TO EMPLOYEES
FROM THE
ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
Case No. S-CA-25-050
The Illinois Labor Relations Board, State Panel, has found that the Chief Judge of the Circuit
Court of Cook County has violated the Illinois Public Labor Relations Act, and has ordered us to
post this Notice. We hereby notify you that the Illinois Public Labor Relations Act (Act) gives
you, as an employee, these rights:
• To engage in self-organization
• To form, join, or assist unions
• To bargain collectively through a representative of your own choosing
• To act together with other employees to bargain collectively or for other
mutual aid or protection
• To refrain from these activities
Accordingly, we assure you that:
WE WILL cease and desist from interfering with, restraining, or coercing the Charging Party in
the exercise of her rights by the Act when the Charging Party requests for a Union
representative during investigatory meetings.
WE WILL cease and desist from retaliating against the Charging Party for protected concerted
activity of requesting a Union representative attend the meeting with her and her supervisors.
WE WILL cease and desist from retaliating against the Charging Party to discourage
membership in or support for the Union.
WE Will cease and desist from in any like or related manner, interfering with, restraining, or
coercing employees in the exercise of the rights guaranteed them under the Act.
WE WILL make Dorothy Ward whole by rescinding the November 14, 2024, verbal reprimand
and removing it from her employment records.
